meta.title: Who really said "If you are going to achieve excellence in big things, you develop the habit in little matters. Excellence is not an exception, it is a prevailing attitude"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Colin Powell almost certainly did. A 2003 leadership book quotes it and cites his 1995 memoir, page 446 — a page we could not open. Attributed, not verified.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1937–2021 · four-star U.S. Army general · Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, 1989–1993 · Secretary of State, 2001–2005
answer.sourceLine: This one is very probably genuine, and it comes with an unusually specific paper trail: Oren Harari’s leadership study The Powell Principles (McGraw-Hill, 2003) prints the sentence as a direct Powell quotation and footnotes it to Powell’s own memoir, My American Journey, written with Joseph E. Persico (Random House, 1995), at page 446. What we could not do is open that page. Every scanned copy of the memoir we could reach is lending-restricted, so the citation remains a very good lead rather than a confirmed reading — which is why this page says “attributed” and not “verified.”
answer.confidenceText: Printed as Powell’s own words in a 2003 book that cites his memoir by page — but that memoir page is behind a lending wall, so the wording is unconfirmed at the primary source.

source.excerpt: If you are going to achieve excellence in big things, you develop the habit in little matters. Excellence is not an exception, it is a prevailing attitude.
trail: Quote Investigator has no file on this line ↗ — a site search returns nothing — so there is no specialist finding to defer to, and no published reason to doubt the attribution either.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the sentence among Powell’s sourced quotes, filed under Oren Harari’s The Powell Principles (2003), with an editor’s note that it evokes Will Durant’s summation of Aristotle.

Harari’s book itself prints the line as a direct Powell quotation, in its lesson on staying vigilant about details, and footnotes it to the memoir My American Journey ↗ — the book Powell wrote with Joseph E. Persico — at page 446.

That page is where the trail stops. The Internet Archive’s scan of the 1995 edition ↗ is lending-restricted, and the other full-text search routes we tried were unavailable, so nobody here has read p. 446 to confirm the exact wording.
source.excerptNote: This is the standard wording, as printed in the lesson text of The Powell Principles. The same book’s epigraph page carries a second version reading “the habit in little things.” Which of the two matches page 446 of the memoir is exactly what an unopened primary source leaves unresolved.

source.rightsNote: Both books in this trail are modern and firmly in copyright: My American Journey was first published in 1995 by Random House, and The Powell Principles in 2003 by McGraw-Hill — decades past the 1931 threshold for U.S. public domain. Quoting a sentence or two for commentary and attribution is ordinary fair use; the books themselves are not free to reproduce.

author.bio: Colin Luther Powell was born in Harlem on 5 April 1937 to Jamaican immigrant parents and rose through the U.S. Army to four stars, serving as National Security Advisor from 1987 to 1989 and as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff from 1989 to 1993 — the youngest officer, and the first Black officer, to hold that post. He later became Secretary of State from 2001 to 2005. His 1995 memoir My American Journey, written with Joseph E. Persico, is the book that leadership writers have mined for his rules ever since; he died on 18 October 2021.

misattribution.heading: How it travels
misattribution.intro: Nobody else claims this sentence — the problem is not a rival author but a missing receipt, and a wording that has already drifted once in print.

items.why: The line is everywhere under Powell’s name with no book, page or date attached. That is the ordinary state of a Powell quotation online, and it is why a sourced citation matters: Wikiquote ↗ is one of the few places that files it against a named book rather than floating it free.

The 2003 book that supplies the standard wording is not internally consistent: its lesson text reads “the habit in little matters,” while a standalone epigraph page in the same volume reads “the habit in little things.” Two wordings inside one book, before the internet had a chance to garble anything — a reminder that the memoir page itself is the wording that should settle it.

Powell’s sentence is frequently quoted alongside — and sometimes merged with — “Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit,” which is routinely printed over Aristotle’s name. Wikiquote sources that line to Will Durant ↗, The Story of Philosophy (1926), p. 87, where he was paraphrasing the Nicomachean Ethics. Powell’s line is his own formulation, not a translation of Aristotle.

misattribution.truthLine: Treat this as Powell’s, with a caveat you can act on: the only page-level citation anyone offers is My American Journey, p. 446, and that page sits inside a lending-restricted scan ↗. If you have a library copy, that page is where the question gets settled.

context.heading: Why a general cared about small things
lead: Powell’s leadership writing keeps returning to the same unglamorous claim: that big outcomes are downstream of small habits, and that a unit which is sloppy about the trivial will be sloppy when it counts. The sentence quoted here is the compressed version of that argument — excellence framed not as a peak performance you summon on the day, but as an ambient standard you have already been practising.

The second half is the part that gets pinned to office walls. “Excellence is not an exception, it is a prevailing attitude” is a claim about culture rather than individuals: it says the thing you are measuring is not how good the best day was, but what the ordinary day looks like when nobody is watching.
detailsBody: The underlying thought is far older than Powell. Wikiquote’s editors flag on his own page that the line evokes Will Durant’s famous summation of Aristotle. Durant’s sentence — “Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit” — appears in The Story of Philosophy (1926), where he was paraphrasing the Nicomachean Ethics for a general readership.

That older line is itself one of the internet’s most reliably mislabelled quotations, routinely printed over Aristotle’s name. Powell’s formulation is a separate sentence in a separate register — a commander’s version rather than a philosopher’s — but the two are close enough that they are often quoted in the same breath, and occasionally blurred into each other.
context.pull: Excellence framed not as a peak you summon, but as the standard you have already been keeping.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the exact quote among Colin Powell's sourced quotes, under the section heading 'The Powell Principles (2003)', with an editor's note that it evokes Will Durant's summation of Aristotle.

The full text of Oren Harari's The Powell Principles prints the quote verbatim in its lesson on details and footnotes it 'Powell, Colin, with Joseph E. Persico, My American Journey (New York: Random House, 1995), p. 446.'; a separate epigraph page in the same book reads 'you develop the habit in little things'.

Colin Powell was born 5 April 1937 and died 18 October 2021; four-star general; National Security Advisor 1987–1989; Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff 1989–1993; Secretary of State 2001–2005; authored My American Journey in 1995.
My American Journey is credited to Colin L. Powell and Joseph E. Persico; the Ballantine Books edition runs 656 pages.
Wikiquote sources 'we are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit' to Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926), p. 87.
A site search of Quote Investigator for 'prevailing attitude' returns no articles — QI has not investigated this quote.
The Internet Archive's scan of the 1995 edition of My American Journey is lending-restricted (Borrow / Log in), so page 446 cannot be read to confirm the wording.
The Powell Principles is by Oren Harari and published by McGraw-Hill.

The 18-lesson 'A Leadership Primer' slide deck attributed to Powell contains this excellence quotation — NOT SUPPORTED: the lesson text extracted from this PDF contains no 'excellence' or 'prevailing' wording, and extraction was partial, so this is not used as evidence either way.
